title: PAUL SAID HUSBAND AND WIFE EACH HAVE AUTHORITY OVER THE OTHER’S BODY—Why Is the Statement Completely MUTUAL?
paragraphs: PAUL SAID HUSBAND AND WIFE EACH HAVE AUTHORITY OVER THE OTHER’S BODY—Why Is the Statement Completely MUTUAL?

One of Paul’s most intimate statements about marriage has been quoted as though it gives one spouse power over the other. But read the sentence Paul actually wrote—and something breathtaking happens: the authority goes both ways. And what comes immediately afterward changes the conversation even more.
There are Bible verses people quote loudly...
and Bible verses people need to read slowly.
First Corinthians 7:4 is one of them.
Because when this verse is pulled out of its context, it can sound frighteningly easy to misuse.
“The wife does not have authority over her own body...”
Stop there, and someone can turn Scripture into a weapon.
Someone can make Christianity sound as though marriage gives a husband unrestricted ownership of his wife.
Someone can even take the sacred language of covenant and use it to silence pain, dismiss fear, or justify selfishness.
But Paul did not stop there.
And neither should we.
Listen to the complete symmetry of what the apostle actually wrote:
ἡ γυνὴ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλὰ ὁ ἀνήρ· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλὰ ἡ γυνή.
Hē gynē tou idiou sōmatos ouk exousiazei alla ho anēr; homoiōs de kai ho anēr tou idiou sōmatos ouk exousiazei alla hē gynē.
In straightforward English:
“The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.”
—1 Corinthians 7:4
Read it again.
Slowly.
Paul does not say the husband has authority over his wife's body while remaining sovereign over his own.
He says something startlingly reciprocal.
Her body is given covenantally to him.
And his body is given covenantally to her.
The Greek verb translated “have authority” is ἐξουσιάζει — exousiazei, from exousiazō, carrying the sense of exercising authority or having authority over something.
But here is what matters enormously:
Paul uses the same idea in both directions.
He doesn't give the husband one verb and the wife another.
He doesn't give the husband authority and then tell the wife merely to cooperate.
The structure mirrors itself.
Wife toward husband.
Husband toward wife.
And sitting right in the middle of Paul's sentence is a word we cannot afford to ignore:
ὁμοίως — homoiōs.
Likewise.
Similarly.
In the same manner.
That single word refuses to let us turn Paul's teaching into a one-way street.
And the surrounding verses make the mutuality even clearer.
Immediately before this, Paul says the husband should give his wife what is due to her, “and likewise” the wife to her husband.
Then immediately after verse 4, Paul says:
μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε ἀλλήλους
“Do not deprive one another.”
Not, “Wives, do not deprive your husbands.”
One another.
Then Paul describes a temporary period of abstinence for prayer and uses another extraordinarily important expression:
ἐκ συμφώνου — ek symphōnou
By agreement.
By mutual consent.
The idea behind symphōnos is agreement or harmony—the same family of thought from which English eventually gets the word “symphony.”
Think about that.
When Paul discusses abstaining within marriage, he does not picture one spouse unilaterally announcing, “You don't have a choice.”
He speaks of agreement.
Mutuality.
Two people acting together.
That matters.
A lot.
Because 1 Corinthians 7:4 was never written to give selfish people a Bible verse with which to dominate their spouse.
It confronts selfishness in both spouses.
Marriage, in Paul's vision, is not two autonomous kingdoms fighting over who gets control.
It is covenantal self-giving.
And that distinction changes everything.
There is an enormous difference between saying,
“Your body belongs to me, therefore I can demand what I want,”
and saying,
“I have given myself to you, therefore I must no longer live as though only my desires matter.”
The first sounds like domination.
The second sounds like covenant.
And Christian covenant is ultimately illuminated by Christ.
Jesus did not love His people by asking, “How much can I take?”
He loved by giving Himself.
Christ's love moves toward sacrifice.
Toward holiness.
Toward faithfulness.
Toward the good of the beloved.
This is why Scripture's vision of marriage cannot honestly be reduced to sexual entitlement.
Marriage is not a divine permission slip for selfishness.
It is one of the places where selfishness is supposed to die.
The husband cannot quote 1 Corinthians 7:4 to his wife while conveniently forgetting that the second half of the exact same verse places his own body under a corresponding covenant obligation.
And the wife cannot use intimacy merely as a weapon of manipulation while ignoring Paul's call to mutual faithfulness and care.
Paul traps selfishness from both directions.
You cannot faithfully read the first half and erase the second.
You cannot shout “authority” while whispering “likewise.”
And you cannot build a theology of coercion while pretending verse 5 does not speak about one another and agreement.
This does not mean married Christians become objects rather than persons.
It does not mean pain becomes irrelevant.
It does not mean illness disappears.
It does not mean trauma should be ignored.
It does not mean fear should be mocked.
It certainly does not turn sexual violence, intimidation, humiliation, or abuse into something holy merely because the perpetrators are married.
Sin does not become righteousness because someone attaches a Bible verse to it.
Jesus never commissioned us to weaponize His Word against the wounded.
Biblical intimacy requires something far deeper than demanding access to another person's body.
It requires becoming the kind of husband or wife with whom vulnerability can be safe.
Maybe that is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because sometimes the real problem in a marriage isn't simply frequency.
Sometimes there are wounds nobody talks about.
A wife feels emotionally abandoned all day and then wonders why she is expected to become instantly vulnerable at night.
A husband experiences rejection repeatedly and quietly begins wondering whether he is still wanted.
One spouse carries exhaustion.
Another carries resentment.
One carries memories from before the marriage that still hurt when touched.
Another carries shame they have never found the courage to explain.
They sleep inches apart...
yet somehow live miles away.
Then somebody quotes a verse.
And instead of Scripture becoming a doorway toward healing, Scripture becomes another wall.
But what if Paul was calling husband and wife away from exactly that kind of selfish isolation?
What if the question isn't merely:
“What does my spouse owe me?”
What if the Gospel forces another question:
“How am I giving myself in love?”
That question reaches far beyond the bedroom.
Husband...
when was the last time your wife felt deeply heard without you immediately trying to defend yourself?
Wife...
when was the last time your husband knew he could reveal weakness without being humiliated for it later?
When was the last time you prayed together without pretending?
When was the last time you apologized without adding “but”?
When was the last time you said:
“I hurt you.”
“I was selfish.”
“I haven't been listening.”
“I've been carrying resentment.”
“I miss us.”
“Forgive me.”
Those words can feel terrifying.
Because intimacy isn't merely naked bodies.
Sometimes the most frightening nakedness is a naked soul.
No excuses.
No performance.
No Christian mask.
Just truth.
And grace.
Maybe you're reading this beside the person you once promised forever to, while privately wondering what happened to the two people who made those promises.
Maybe nobody knows.
At church, you smile.
The photographs still look beautiful.
The anniversary posts still sound romantic.
People may even call you a wonderful Christian couple.
But behind the closed door...
silence.
Distance.
Resentment.
Temptation.
Unspoken disappointment.
Maybe one of you stopped reaching because rejection hurt too much.
Maybe the other stopped responding because years of emotional neglect hollowed something out.
Maybe pornography entered the marriage.
Maybe infidelity did.
Maybe harsh words did.
Maybe work became an escape.
Maybe ministry became an escape.
Maybe you learned how to coexist without really knowing each other anymore.
And now a verse about bodies feels almost painfully ironic because the deeper truth is this:
Your bodies may still share a house while your hearts have stopped sharing a home.
If that sentence hurts, don't run from the pain too quickly.
Bring it to Jesus.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of people who never broke anything.
It is the story of a Savior who redeems sinners.
Jesus Christ came for people carrying real shame.
Real lust.
Real betrayal.
Real selfishness.
Real wounds.
Real failure.
Real sin.
The cross doesn't tell us our sin was insignificant.
The cross tells us our sin was so serious that Christ died—and His grace so astonishing that He willingly did.
Repentance therefore isn't humiliation for humiliation's sake.
Repentance is coming into the light.
It is stopping the blame game.
It is laying down the weapon.
It is saying:
“Jesus, show me where I have become selfish.”
Not merely...
“Jesus, fix my spouse.”
Maybe the husband needs to repent.
Maybe the wife needs to repent.
Maybe both do.

Maybe one has committed grave wrong against the other, and repentance will require more than emotional words—it will require truth, changed behavior, accountability, patience, and the rebuilding of trust.
Forgiveness is not pretending evil was good.
Grace is not calling abuse love.
Reconciliation cannot be manufactured through religious pressure.
And where there is abuse, coercion, violence, or danger, seeking safety and trustworthy pastoral, professional, and where necessary legal help is not spiritual failure.
But for the ordinary selfishness that slowly suffocates so many marriages, Paul's words still pierce deeply.
Your marriage cannot thrive indefinitely when everything becomes:
My needs.
My schedule.
My exhaustion.
My pleasure.
My wounds.
My preferences.
My rights.
My body.
My way.
Because Christian marriage keeps colliding with two terrifyingly beautiful words:
one another.
Love one another.
Serve one another.
Forgive one another.
Bear with one another.
And here in 1 Corinthians 7...
do not deprive one another.
The Gospel keeps turning “me” toward “we.”
Not by erasing individuality.
Not by sanctifying control.
But by crucifying selfishness.
And this is where 1 Corinthians 7:4 begins sounding less like a verse about what you are allowed to take...
and more like a verse about what covenant love is willing to give.
Your spouse is not merchandise.
Your spouse is not a machine designed to satisfy you.
Your spouse is not your enemy.
And your spouse is certainly not your savior.
Jesus is.
That matters because no husband can carry the weight of being his wife's Messiah.
No wife can carry the weight of being her husband's Messiah.
Marriage makes promises human beings should keep.
But only Christ can rescue the human heart from sin.
Only Christ can cleanse guilt.
Only Christ can give a new heart.
Only Christ can restore what repentance places into His hands.
So if your marriage is hurting, don't merely fight harder for control.
Run toward Christ.
If you've sinned sexually, confess.
If you've been selfish, repent.
If you've become cold, ask God to expose why.
If you've wounded your spouse, stop demanding that they “get over it” and begin becoming trustworthy.
If you've been hiding something, bring darkness into light.
And if your marriage is healthy...
don't become careless.
Protect it.
Pray over it.
Treasure it.
Keep choosing each other.
Keep communicating.
Keep laughing.
Keep touching.
Keep forgiving.
Keep pursuing Christ together.
Because the enemy does not need every marriage to explode publicly.
Sometimes he is perfectly satisfied watching one die quietly.
And maybe someone reading this tonight needs to hear:
It doesn't have to remain this way.
Not because every marriage story automatically receives the ending we want.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because another person's choices can be controlled.
But because Jesus still transforms people who truly surrender to Him.
The Gospel still reaches adulterers.
The Gospel still reaches the sexually broken.
The Gospel still reaches selfish husbands.
The Gospel still reaches resentful wives.
The Gospel still reaches pornography addicts.
The Gospel still reaches people drowning in shame.
The Gospel still reaches people who thought they had gone too far.
That is Christianity's scandalous announcement:
Your worst chapter does not have greater authority than the blood of Jesus Christ.
Repent.
Come home.
Receive grace.
And then walk differently.
Maybe this article exposed something you have been hiding.
Talk to Jesus.
And then, where appropriate and safe, have the conversation you've been avoiding.
Say the apology.
Tell the truth.
Ask for help.
Seek wise counsel.
Open the Scriptures together.
Pray.
No performance.
No pretending.
Sometimes three words are enough to admit that you need grace.
And somebody else reading those words may realize they aren't the only one struggling.
Because marriage has seasons, and there may come a night when you need to read these words again.
Scripture calls believers to generosity that is willing rather than coerced: “not reluctantly or under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
That is exactly how we want your support to be.
Freely given.
Christ-centered.
For the spread of biblical truth.
don't miss the greater invitation.
Give yourself to Christ.
No donation can buy forgiveness.
No ministry membership can reconcile you to God.
Jesus already paid that price.
And perhaps that is the deepest lesson hidden inside this controversial passage.
The Gospel never teaches us to ask first:
“What can I take?”
At the cross, we encounter the Savior who gave Himself.
And when that Gospel reaches a marriage, husband and wife begin learning the same holy rhythm:
Not domination.
Not manipulation.
Not selfish entitlement.
But covenant faithfulness.
Mutual care.
Sacrificial love.
Repentance when we fail.
Grace when we return.
And Jesus at the center of it all.
Because perhaps the marriage you thought was only becoming another story of wounds and disappointment is standing at the doorway of a different chapter...
and the hand holding the pen still bears nail scars.
What selfishness tried to destroy, surrender can finally place into the hands of the Savior who still writes resurrection into ruined chapters.
